title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Finding the slow parts
Different parts of the code are differently fast.
Profiling means that we run the program and measure how much time is spent in each function.
A good way to do this is to use the cProfile module.
Another option is to use a line profiler - we will look at this later.

Measuring execution time
Simplest way - using the time module

import time

start = time.time()

# Do some work
import numpy as np

s = np.sum(np.arange(1000_000))
print("The sum is ", s)

end = time.time()
print(f"Calculating the sum took {end - start:.4f} seconds")



Problems

execution time varies
lots of noise, especially if the operation you are measuring is fast



Better - use the timeit module
The timeit.timeit method gives you more reliable measurements.
It has several keyword arguments.
timeit.timeit(stmt='pass', setup='pass', number=1000000)

setup is executed before the stmt that is timed,
number is the number of repetitions.


For other timeit methods, consult the course book.

import numpy as np
import timeit

repetitions = 1000

total_execution_time = timeit.timeit(
    "sum(arange(1_000_000))",
    number=repetitions,
    setup="from numpy import sum, arange"
)

print(f"Calculating the sum took {total_execution_time / repetitions:.6f} seconds on average")




Even better - use the %timeit IPython magic

Automatically determines number of repetitions neccessary to get statistically significant results
The %timeit magic is ideal for measuring execution time of short statements
Only avaliable in the IPython console!

From the IPython console
In [1]: %timeit np.sum(np.arange(1000_000))
Or from the terminal
$ python -m timeit --setup "import numpy as np" "np.sum(np.arange(1000_000))"
Note that in the above a --setup argument is passed to import numpy before running the measurement.

%timeit np.sum(np.arange(1000_000))

Note that this last measurement is lower than the two previous… why is that?


Example - moving average
Consider a sequence \(a_i\) for \(i=0..N-1\).
The moving average of the last 3 values is \(m_j(a) = \frac{1}{3}\sum_{i=j}^{j+2} a_i\), for \(j=1..N-2\).

def moving_average(a):
    N = len(a)
    m = np.zeros(N-2)
    for j in range(len(m)):
        m[j] = (a[j] + a[j+1] + a[j+2]) / 3
    return m

a = [1, 0, 0, 1, 0]
moving_average(a)


# Use a big array when timing.
a = np.random.randn(10000)
%timeit moving_average(a)

Can we do better?
Try using a list comprehension:

def moving_average_comp(a):
    N = len(a)
    return np.array([(a[j] + a[j+1] + a[j+2]) / 3
                     for j in range(N-2)])

%timeit moving_average_comp(a)
print(a)

Can we do better?
Remember that vectorized operations on Numpy arrays are fast!

def moving_average_vec(a):
    return (a[:-2] + a[1:-1] + a[2:]) / 3

%timeit moving_average_vec(a)
print(a)



Takeaway: Numpy vector operations vs. for loop
Numpy arrays are optimized for storing numbers and doing calculations.
Python lists are optimized to be flexible storage for any kinds of objects.

Use vectorized operations when you can.
But don’t use them if they make the code more complicated.

“First make it work - then make it fast” priciple.




Example - pow vs. mul
Is there a difference in performance between multiplication and squaring?

a = np.random.rand(10000)
%timeit a * a
%timeit a**2
%timeit a**2.0
%timeit a**2.1



Example - common mistake!
The built-in Python sum function is not aware of the difference between Python iterables (list, tuple, etc.) and Numpy arrays.

# from numpy import *
import numpy as np
b = np.random.randn(10000)
%timeit np.sum(b)
%timeit sum(b)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
How to profile larger programs?
Execution time of a single function can be checked using timeit. But in some cases it is more useful to get an overview of where time is spent.
One tool to get this overview is line-profiling. This is advanced, but you might find it useful in your projects.

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Golden rules
Avoid premature optimization.
Measure. Then optimize.

Setup
Run in the IPython console
!pip install line_profiler
%load_ext line_profiler

See here for more great profiling tools https://jakevdp.github.io/PythonDataScienceHandbook/01.07-timing-and-profiling.html

!pip install line_profiler
%load_ext line_profiler




Using %lprun
The line profiler is used to measure how much time is spent on each line of function.
Particularly useful for detecting unexpected expensive operations.

The -f argument selects which function to investigate
The last argument is the statement to be executed

In [1]: %lprun -f name_of_function run_program()

import numpy as np
def bisect(f, a, b, tol=1.e-8):
    if f(a) * f(b) > 0:
        raise ValueError("Incorrect initial [a , b ]")
    for i in range(100):
        c = (a + b) / 2.
        if f(a) * f(c) <= 0:
            b = c
        else:
            a = c
        if abs(a - b) < tol:
            return (a + b) / 2
    raise Exception("No root found")
    
def main():
    bisect(lambda x: (x + 1) * x, -1, 1)
    bisect(lambda x: np.exp(x) - 1, -1, 1)
    bisect(lambda x: 4 - x, 2, 6)


%load_ext line_profiler
%lprun -f bisect main()

Decorators
def decorator(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print("Before calling function.")
        val = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print("After calling function.")
        return val
    # Return a new function with extended functionality.
    return wrapper
A decorator is a function that extends the functionality of another function.

def decorator(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print("Before calling function.")
        val = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print("After calling function.")
        return val
    return wrapper

    print("Greetings from f(x)!")

Example (cont)
Consider the two functions:

from numpy import array 
def shift_using_loop(vec):
    V = vec.copy()  # make a copy to keep vec intact
    n = len(V)
    for i in range(n-1, 0, -1):  # we must do this in reverse order
        V[i] = V[i-1]
    return V

def shift_using_slices(vec):
    V = vec.copy()
    V[1:] = V[:-1]
    return V

n = 10

L = list(range(n))
L1 = shift_using_loop(L)
L2 = shift_using_slices(L)

A = array(list(range(n)))
A1 = shift_using_loop(A)
A2 = shift_using_slices(A)

print(L)
print(L1)

The rectangular region is specified using a relative coordinate system.

title: GUI using matplotlib
text:
The show() command
If running a Python program from an editor that doesn’t have an IPython console, or if running it in a terminal:
python example1.py
you must show a plot by using the matplotlib function
show()

title: GUI using matplotlib
text:
Example 1 - One slider
The graph of \(f(x) = A\sin(x)\).
We will use a slider for the value of the amplitude \(A\).
Import the Slider class (and for later, the Button class).
from matplotlib.widgets import Slider, Button
Make a figure object and the axes objects for the slider and the plot:
fig = figure()

# layout
sld_ax = axes([0.2, 0.9, 0.6, 0.05])  # axes for slider
ax = axes([0.1, 0.15, 0.8, 0.7])      # axes for the plot
Make the slider.
sld = Slider(sld_ax, 'amp', 0., 5.)
You can also use keyword arguments.
sld = Slider(sld_ax, 'amp', 0., 5., 
             valinit=1, valstep=0.1, valfmt="%1.1f")
The value of the slider will be stored in sld.val.
Make \(x\)-values and format the plot.
x = linspace(-2*pi, 2*pi, 200)
ax.set_ylim(-5.5, 5.5)  # why is this needed in this case
Make the plot and get a reference to the line plot object.
lines, = ax.plot(x, sld.val*sin(x))
Define a callback function and use it as argument for the event handler.
def update_amplitude(val):
    lines.set_ydata(val*sin(x))
    
sld.on_changed(update_amplitude)
The parameter val holds the value of the slider. You could also use sld.val when setting the ydata.

Note that your callback function only can have one single parameter.
Note that your callback function changes a global variable. This can be avoided by enclosing the code in a class.

text:
Example 1: The full program
Make sure all imports have been made:

from numpy import *
from matplotlib.pyplot import *
from matplotlib.widgets import Slider, Button
%matplotlib notebook


fig = figure(figsize = (8,3))
ax = axes([0.1, 0.15, 0.8, 0.7])     # axes for the plot
ax.set_ylim(-5.5, 5.5)

sld_ax = axes([0.2, 0.9, 0.6, 0.05]) # axes for slider
sld = Slider(sld_ax, 'amp', 0., 5.)

x = linspace(-2*pi, 2*pi, 200)
lines, = ax.plot(x, sld.val*sin(x))

def update_amplitude( A ):
    lines.set_ydata(A*sin(x))
    
sld.on_changed(update_amplitude);  # ; to suppress Out[xx]

section: Example 2 - A button and a slider
text:
Example 2 - A button and a slider
We will again use
\[f(x) = A\sin(x).\]

A slider has a on_changed event handler.
A button has a on_clicked event handler.

Let the slider hold the value of the amplitude of a sine-curve. Let the button, not the slider, show the updated curve.
In this case the button is meaningless. For cases where lengthy calculations are performed when sliders change values, it’s better not to use the on_changed event to update plots.

title: GUI using matplotlib
text:
Example 2: The full program

fig = figure(figsize = (8, 3))      
sld_ax = axes([0.2, 0.9, 0.6, 0.05])  # axes for slider
btn_ax = axes([0.7, 0.8, 0.2, 0.07])  # axes for button
ax = axes([0.1, 0.15, 0.8, 0.6])      # axes for the plot
sld = Slider(sld_ax, 'amp', 0., 5.)
btn = Button(btn_ax, 'Show curve')    
x = linspace(-2*pi, 2*pi, 200)
ax.set_ylim(-5.5, 5.5)
lines, = ax.plot(x, sld.val*sin(x))

def show_curve(event):
    lines.set_ydata(sld.val*sin(x))  # the amplitude is given by the slider value
    
btn.on_clicked(show_curve);
show()

title: GUI using matplotlib
section: Example 3 - Two sliders in a list
text:
Example 3 - Two sliders in a list
For the damped Lissajous curve defined by
\[
\begin{cases}
        x(t) &= \cos(at)e^{-dt} \\
        y(t) &= \sin(t)e^{-dt}
    \end{cases}
    , 0\leq t \lt 14\pi
\]
use one slider for the angular frequency \(a\) and one for the damping factor \(d\).

Two sliders in a list
Two sliders are fairly easy to handle. If many sliders are needed, the code will be shorter if the layout is made in some loop.
To make a slider, we use:
sld = Slider(sld_ax, label, valmin, valmax)
For our two values, \(a\in[0, 2]\) and \(d\in[0, 0.1]\)
Our two values will have different labels and different valmax values.


A function for making sliders in a list
def make_sliders(labels, valmaxs):
    sliders = []
    for i in range(2):
        sld_ax = axes([0.05, 0.4+0.1*i, 0.28, 0.03])
        sld = Slider(sld_ax, labels[i], 0, valmaxs[i])
        sliders.append(sld)
    return sliders
It is easy to afterwards change the layout of all sliders.
To make the list of sliders, we use:
sld = make_sliders(['a', 'd'], [2, 0.1])


The callback function
We use the same callback function for both sliders
def update_curve(val):
    a, d = sld[0].val, sld[1].val
    line.set_xdata(cos(a*t)*exp(-d*t))
    line.set_ydata(sin(t)*exp(-d*t))
for s in sld:
    s.on_changed(update_curve)
If we had many sliders in a list and a callback function depending on the index of a list element, we could use a closure to make a function with only one parameter.
def outer(i):
    def inner(val):
        # code using i and val
    return inner
for i in range(len(sld)):
    s.on_changed(outer(i))


Make the axes for the initial plot
ax = axes([0.5, 0.1, 0.5, 0.8])
ax.set_xlim([-1, 1])
ax.set_ylim([-1, 1])
ax.set_aspect(1.0)  # the aspect ratio should be 1 in this case

a, d = sld[0].val, sld[1].val
line, = ax.plot(cos(a*t)*exp(-d*t), sin(t)*exp(-d*t))

title: GUI using matplotlib
text:
Example 3: The full program
Assuming all imports have been made. The two functions:

def make_sliders(labels, valmaxs):
    sliders = []
    for i in range(2):
        sld_ax = axes([0.05, 0.4+0.1*i, 0.28, 0.03])
        sld = Slider(sld_ax, labels[i], 0, valmaxs[i])

def update_curve(val):
    a, d = sld[0].val, sld[1].val

    line.set_ydata(sin(t)*exp(-d*t))


fig = figure(figsize=(8, 3))
sld = make_sliders(['a', 'd'], [2, 0.1])

title: GUI using matplotlib
text:
Events
Matplotlib has an event manager that can handle mouse events (and some other events).
To handle an event:

Write a callback function
Connect the callback function to the event manager.

If your callback function updates a plot, you must use
fig.canvas.draw_idle()  # redraws the canvas

title: GUI using matplotlib
text:
The callback function
Assuming there is a figure object fig:
def my_callback(event):
    # code
    
cid = fig.canvas.mpl_connect('button_press_event', my_callback)
cid stands for connection id. If you want to disconnect your callback use:
fig.canvas.mpl_disconnect(cid)
You could also use other mouse events: 'button_released_event', 'motion_notify_event', 'scroll_event'.

title: GUI using matplotlib
text:
The callback function (cont)
def my_callback(event):
    # code
    
cid = fig.canvas.mpl_connect('button_press_event', my_callback)
The parameter event has attributes that you can use in your callback function.

event.xdata       the \(x\)-coordinate of the mouse in data coordinates
event.ydata       the \(y\)-coordinate of the mouse in data coordinates
event.inaxes     the axes object where the event occurred
event.button     1 = left click, 2 = middle click, 3 = right click

title: GUI using matplotlib
text:
A simple example
This code works in Spyder (but not in a notebook):

fig, ax = subplots()

def my_callback(event):
    if event.inaxes == ax:
        x = event.xdata
        y = event.ydata
        print(f"x={x:0.2f}, y={y:0.2f}")

cid = fig.canvas.mpl_connect('button_press_event', my_callback)

title: GUI using matplotlib
section: Example 4 - Click to make points and a spline
text:
Example 4 - Click to make points and a spline
As long as the user left clicks in the plotting area, a new point will be made.
The points will be in a line plot that is an empty line plot when the program starts.
When all points have been made, a spline will be created from the points.
 (Image of spline from Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_spline) 

Make two empty line plots and lists for storing coordinates
fig, ax = subplots()

points, = ax.plot([], [], 'or')  # line plot of red points
lines, = ax.plot([], [], '-b')   # line plot for a blue spline
xlist, ylist = [], []            # lists for storing coordinates


Make a callback function using global variables
def onclick(event):
    if event.inaxes == ax:
        if event.button == 1:
            xlist.append(event.xdata)
            ylist.append(event.ydata)
            points.set_xdata(xlist)
            points.set_ydata(ylist)
        else:
            fig.canvas.mpl_disconnect(cid)
        fig.canvas.draw_idle()

cid = fig.canvas.mpl_connect('button_press_event', onclick)
To avoid having to use global variables, make a class.


Example 4: Click to make points

fig, ax = subplots(figsize=(8, 2))
points, = ax.plot([], [], 'or')  # line plot of red points
lines, = ax.plot([], [], '-b')   # line plot for the blue spline
xlist, ylist = [], []            # lists for storing coordinates
def onclick(event):
    if event.inaxes == ax:
        if event.button == 1:
            xlist.append(event.xdata)
            ylist.append(event.ydata)
            points.set_xdata(xlist)
            points.set_ydata(ylist)
        else:
            fig.canvas.mpl_disconnect(cid)
        fig.canvas.draw_idle()
cid = fig.canvas.mpl_connect('button_press_event', onclick)



Making a spline
The scipy package interpolate has several functions and classes for making splines.

from scipy.interpolate import splprep, splev

To make a B-spline (basic spline) as a parametric curve: - get a representation of the spline using splprep - use the representation of the spline to evaluate the spline using splev
This procedure resembles the procedure to fit a polynomial to data: use numpy polyfit to get coefficients, use polyval with the coefficients to make the polynomial.


Making a spline (cont)

Using splprep
tck, u = interpolate.splprep([x, y], s=0)
where

tck is a tuple containing the vector of knots, the B-spline coefficients, and the degree of the spline.
u is an array of parameter values (for the parametric curve).

If the keyword argument s=0(s stand for smoothness) is given, the spline will go through the points. It is possible to make a closed curve by providing the keyword argument per=1. In that case, the first list element should be the same as the last list element for the lists x and y (use append).


Using splev
xvalues, yvalues = splev(linspace(0, 1, 100), tck)
xvalues and yvalues can be used for making a plot. The first argument is an array of parameter values. If u (from splprep) is used as first argument, line segments will be drawn between the points.



Example 4: The full program

fig, ax = subplots(figsize=(8, 2))
points, = ax.plot([], [], 'or')
lines, = ax.plot([], [], '-b')
xlist, ylist = [], []
def onclick(event):
    if event.inaxes == ax:
        if event.button == 1:
            xlist.append(event.xdata)
            ylist.append(event.ydata)
            points.set_xdata(xlist)
            points.set_ydata(ylist)
        else:
            tck, u = splprep([xlist, ylist], s=0)
            xi, yi = splev(linspace(0, 1, 100), tck)
            lines.set_xdata(xi)
            lines.set_ydata(yi)
            fig.canvas.mpl_disconnect(cid)
        fig.canvas.draw_idle()
cid = fig.canvas.mpl_connect('button_press_event', onclick)

title: Computational Programming with Python
Computational Programming with Python
text:
Everything can be changed
By default all members in a Python class are public. Any member can be accessed from outside the class environment. Everything can be changed after creating an instance.
In other programming languages such as C++ or Java there exist concepts for public, protected and private members in a class.

r = RationalNumber(2, 3)
print(r)
r.numerator = 23
r.name = 'my favorite fraction' # a new attribute
print(r)
print(r.name)

We can even delete an attribute.

r = RationalNumber(2, 3)
del r.numerator
print(r)  # error

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
A similar class
Consider following class:

from numpy import gcd
class SimplifiedFraction:
    # greatest_common_divisor = 0
    def __init__(self, num, denom): 
        greatest_common_divisor = gcd(num, denom) # using the numpy function gcd()
        self.num = int(num/greatest_common_divisor)
        self.denom = int(denom/greatest_common_divisor)
    
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"{self.num}/{self.denom}"
        # return str(self.num) + "/" + str(self.denom)
    
p = SimplifiedFraction(3, 12)
print("p =", p)

p.num = 2        # here the numerator is changed
print("p =", p)  # no longer a simplified fraction

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Changing attributes
We can protect access to attributes. By convention attributes that have a leading underscore are meant for internal use only.

from numpy import gcd
class SimplifiedFraction:
    def __init__(self, num, denom): 
        greatest_common_divisor = gcd(num, denom)  
        self._num = int(num/greatest_common_divisor)
        self._denom = int(denom/greatest_common_divisor)
    
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"{self._num}/{self._denom}"
    
p = SimplifiedFraction(3, 12)
p._num = 2
# p = SimplifiedFraction.__init__(p,3,12)
print("p =", p)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Get and set
We can provide getter and setter methods to replace direct access.

class SimplifiedFraction:
    def __init__(self, num, denom): 
        greatest_common_divisor = gcd(num, denom)  
        self._num = int(num/greatest_common_divisor)
        self._denom = int(denom/greatest_common_divisor)
        
    def get_num(self):
        return self._num
    
    def set_num(self, new_num):
        self.__init__(new_num, self._denom)  # simplify the new fraction
    
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"{self._num}/{self._denom}"
    
p = SimplifiedFraction(3, 12)

print("p =", p)
print(p._num) # bad style, don't do it
print(p.get_num()) # good style, do it like this

p.set_num(2)    # using the setter 
print("p =", p)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
A triangle example



triangle

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
A class implementing a triangle

from numpy import array, cross
class Triangle:
    def __init__(self, A, B, C):
        self.A = array(A)
        self.B = array(B)
        self.C = array(C)
        self.a = self.C - self.B
        self.b = self.C - self.A
        self.c = self.B - self.A
    def area(self):
        return abs(cross([*self.b,0], [*self.c,0]))[-1]/2 # the numpy cross function
    
tr = Triangle([0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1])
print("area =", tr.area())

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
The cross function
For vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), the cross product is returned.

a = array([1, 0, 0])
b = array([0, 1, 0])
print(cross(a, b))

For vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the \(z\) component is assumed to be zero, and the \(z\) component of the cross product is returned.

a = array([1, 0])
b = array([0, 1])
print(cross(a, b))

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Altering an attribute
In the triangle example, attributes depend on each other. Altering an attribute can cause data inconsistencies:

tr = Triangle([0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1])
print("area =", tr.area())
tr.B = array([10, 0])
print("area =", tr.area())  # wrong area

title: Computational Programming with Python
section: Using getter and setter methods for B
text:
Using getter and setter methods for B

class Triangle:
    def __init__(self, A, B, C):
        self._A = array(A)
        self._B = array(B)
        self._C = array(C)
        self._a = self._C - self._B
        self._b = self._C - self._A
        self._c = self._B - self._A
    def area(self):
        return abs(cross([*self._b, 0], [*self._c, 0]))[-1]/2
    def get_B(self):
        return self._B
    def set_B(self, B):
        self._B = array(B)
        self._a = self._C - self._B
        self._c = self._B - self._A
        # or simply use init again
        # self.__init__(self._A, B, self._C)

Now we can use the methods get_B and set_B to access the attribute B.

tr = Triangle([0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1])
tr.set_B([10, 0])
print("area =", tr.area())  # correct area

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
The property command
We can bind the getter and setter methods to a property B. The property B is accessed directly but internally the getter and setter methods will use the hidden attribute _B.

title: Computational Programming with Python
Computational Programming with Python
text:
A common mistake ‐ underscore forgotten

class Triangle:
    def __init__(self, A, B, C):
        self._A = array(A)
        self._B = array(B)
        self._C = array(C)
        self._a = self._C - self._B
        self._b = self._C - self._A
        self._c = self._B - self._A
    def area(self):
        return abs(cross(self._b, self._c))/2
    def _get_B(self):
        return self._B           # should be self._B otherwise we get a RecursionError
    def _set_B(self, B):
        self._B = B
        self._a = self._C - self._B
        self._c = self._B - self._A
    B = property(fget=_get_B, fset=_set_B)

What happens if we try to run:

tr = Triangle([0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1])
print(tr.B)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
A triangle has three corners
Python allows us to delete an attribute. If so, we won’t have a triangle any more. To prohibit deletion:

%%script python --no-raise-error
from numpy import *
class Triangle:
    def __init__(self, A, B, C):
        self._A = array(A)
        self._B = array(B)
        self._C = array(C)
        self._a = self._C - self._B
        self._b = self._C - self._A
        self._c = self._B - self._A
    def area(self):
        return abs(cross(self._b, self._c))/2
    def get_B(self):
        return self._B 
    def set_B(self, B):
        self._B = B
        self._a = self._C - self._B
        self._c = self._B - self._A
    def del_Pt(self):
        raise Exception("A triangle point cannot be deleted.")
    B = property(fget=get_B, fset=set_B, fdel=del_Pt)
    
tr = Triangle([0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1])
del tr.B

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Defining the base class

from matplotlib.pyplot import plot, grid
class Line:
    def __init__(self, A, B):
        self.A = array(A)
        self.B = array(B)   
    def plot(self):
        grid()
        plot([self.A[0], self.B[0]], [self.A[1], self.B[1]])
        
L = Line([1, 1], [5, 3])
L.plot()

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Defining a derived class DashedLine
A DashedLine inherits all data attributes and all methods from Line but the plot method is redefined, overriding the method of the base class.

class DashedLine(Line):
    def plot(self):  # override the plot method
        # super().plot()
        plot([self.A[0], self.B[0]], [self.A[1], self.B[1]], '--')
        
li = Line([1, 1], [5, 3])
#li.plot()
dl = DashedLine([1, 1], [5, 3])  
print(f"dl.A = {dl.A}, dl.B = {dl.B}")
dl.plot()  
#if isinstance(dl, Line): 
#    dl.plot()

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Using super()
We can make another derived class NonVerticalLine. It has the same attributes as Line, but also the attributes slope and y_intercept.
To call the __init__ method of the parent class, we refer to the parent class by using super().

class NonVerticalLine(Line):
    def __init__(self, A, B):     # override the init method 
        super().__init__(A, B) 
        self.slope = (B[1]-A[1])/(B[0]-A[0]) # may raise a ZeroDivisionError
        self.y_intercept = A[1] - self.slope*A[0]
        
L = NonVerticalLine([-1, -1], [4, 1])
print(f"L.A = {L.A}, L.B = {L.B}, L.slope = {L.slope}, L.y_intercept = {L.y_intercept}")
L.plot()

title: Computational Programming with Python
section: Adding a linear function as a method
text:
Adding a linear function as a method
We can add the function \(f(x) = mx +c\), where \(m\) is the slope and \(c\) the \(y\)-intercept, as a method for the class NonVerticalLine.

class NonVerticalLine(Line):
    def __init__(self, A, B):
        super().__init__(A, B) 
        self.slope = (B[1]-A[1])/(B[0]-A[0])    
        self.y_intercept = A[1] - self.slope*A[0]
        
    def f(self, x):
        return self.slope*x + self.y_intercept
    
L = NonVerticalLine([0, 0], [2, 4])
L.plot()
print("f(100) =", L.f(100))

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
isinstance and issubclass
A non-vertical line is also a line.

L = NonVerticalLine([1, 2], [2, 4])

print(isinstance(L, Line))
print(isinstance(L, NonVerticalLine))
print(isinstance(L, DashedLine))

We can check if a class is a derived class of another class

print(issubclass(NonVerticalLine, Line))  # NonVerticalLine is a subclass of Line
print(issubclass(Line, NonVerticalLine))  # Line is not a subclass of NonVerticalLine

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Objects that act like functions (cont)
We can make a class that has a f method corresponding to a function value.

class Sin:
    def __init__(self, A, omega):
        self._A = A
        self._omega = omega
    
    def f(self, x):
        return self._A*sin(self._omega*x)
    
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"{self._A}*sin({self._omega}x)"
    
sin1 = Sin(1, 1)
sin2 = Sin(2, 0.5)
print(sin1)
print(sin2)

a = quad(sin1.f, 0, pi)
b = quad(sin2.f, 0, pi)

print(a)
print(b)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
The special method __call__
Using __call__, we can call an instance just like we would call a function.

from numpy import *
from scipy.integrate import quad
class Sin:
    def __init__(self, A, omega):
        self._A = A
        self._omega = omega
    
    def __call__(self, x):  # easier to use than the previous value method 
        return self._A*sin(self._omega*x)
    
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"{self._A}*sin({self._omega}x)"
    
sin1 = Sin(1, 1)
sin2 = Sin(2, 0.5)
print(sin1(pi/2))   # print sin at position pi/2, here __call__ is executed
print(sin2(pi))

a = quad(sin1, 0, pi)  # sin1.__call__ is used
b = quad(sin2, 0, pi)

print(a)
print(b)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Arithmetic operators for functions
In mathematics we can add functions.
\[
f(x) = \sin(x) \\
g(x) = \cos(x) \\
h(x) = f(x) + g(x)
\]
In Python this is not directly possible:

%%script python --no-raise-error
from numpy import *
f = sin
g = cos
h = f + g  # error

With the concept of classes, we can program an elegant work-around.
\[
f(x) = \sin(x) \\
g(x) = \cos(x) \\
h(x) = f(x) + g(x)
\]
Implement a class Function that evaluates a given function on __call__ and can __add__ two Function objects to accommodate the above statement.
5min, let’s go!

# TODO: Implement Function
class Function:
    pass


class Function:                 # encapsulate a function
    def __init__(self, f):
        self._f = f 
    def __call__(self, x):
        return self._f(x)
    def __add__(self, g):
        def sum(x):
            return self(x)+g(x)
        return type(self)(sum)  # return an instance of the same class
        # return 
       
f = Function(sin)
g = Function(cos)
h = f + g
x = linspace(-pi, pi)
plot(x, f(x), '--', x, g(x), '--', x, h(x))

title: Computational Programming with Python

Making a static method
Instead of using the numpy gcd function, we could write one using Euclid’s algorithm:

def my_gcd(a, b):
    while b != 0:
        print(f"{a} = {a//b}*{b} + {a%b}")
        a, b = b, a%b
    return a

print(my_gcd(120, 25))
print(20*"-")
print(my_gcd(25, 120))

Making a class method
A vertical line can be defined by one point only. We could add a method for making a vertical line.

class Line:
    # clsVar = 1
    def __init__(self, A, B):
        self.A = array(A)
        self.B = array(B)   
    def plot(self):
        grid()
        plot([self.A[0], self.B[0]], [self.A[1], self.B[1]])
        
    @classmethod
    def make_vertical_line(cls, A):  # the parameter cls refers to the class Line
        # cls.clsVar += 1
        B = array([A[0], A[1]+1])
        return cls(A, B)
        
L1 = Line([1, 1], [5, 3])
L2 = Line.make_vertical_line([2, 1])
L1.plot()
L2.plot()

    def instMth( self , x ): # the first arg is the inst

Class methods are in the namespace of a class and can access the class through a parameter cls.
Static methods are in the namespace of a class but cannot access neither the class nor an instance.

The words self and cls are not reserved words but conventions.

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Comparing floating point numbers
Operations on floating point numbers rarely return the exact result:

a = 0.4 - 0.3
print(f"{a:2.18f}")

This fact matters when comparing floating point numbers:

(0.4 - 0.3) == 0.1

Never compare floats using ==. Ask instead if they are near:

abs((0.4 - 0.3) - 0.1) < 1e-13


from numpy import exp, inf, nan # not a number
#print(exp(1000.))
a = inf
print(3 - a)
print(3 + a)
print(a + a)
print(a - a)
print(a / a)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Internal representation
Floats are represented by three quantities: The sign, the significand (or mantissa) and the exponent: \[
\text{sign}(x) \left( x_0 + x_1 \beta^{-1} + \dots + x_{t-1} \beta^{-(t-1)} \right) \beta^k, \quad \beta \in \mathbb{N}, \quad x_0 \neq 0, \quad 0 \leq x_i < \beta.
\]

\(x_0, \dots, x_{t-1}\) is the significand,
\(t\) is the length of the significand,
\(\beta\) is the basis,
\(k\) is the exponent with \(|k| \leq k_{max}\).

Normalization \(x_0 \neq 0\) makes the representation unique (and saves one bit in the case \(\beta = 2\) and allows to add \(x_t \beta^{-t}\)).
On your computer for a normal float (double): - \(\beta = 2\), - \(t = 52\), - \(k_{max} = 1023\) (which needs 10 bits).
Together with the sign and the full range (sign) of the exponent, this requires 64 bits.

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Internal representation (cont.)
We then have the following representation (adding \(x_t \beta^{-t}\) because \(x_0\) is fixed): \[
(-1)^{\text{sign}} \left( \underbrace{1}_{= x_0} + \sum_{i=1}^{t} x_i 2^{-i}\right) 2^k, \quad x_i \in \{0,1\}.
\]
\(0\) cannot be represented as a normalized float.
Two zeroes: All the exponent bits \(0\) with all significand bits \(0\) represents \(0\). If sign bit is \(0\), then we have \(0\), else \(-0\).
Infinity: All the exponent bits \(1\) with all significand bits \(0\) represents infinity.
Denormalized number: All the exponent bits \(0\) and significand bits non-zero represents denormalized number.
Error: All the exponent bits \(1\) and significand bits non-zero represents error or nan (Not a Number).

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Precision – Machine epsilon

Definition (Maching epsilon):
The machine epsilon or rounding unit is the gap between \(1.0\) and the next larger floating point number, i.e. the largest number \(\epsilon\) such that \[
\mathrm{float}(1.0 + \epsilon) = 1.0
\]
Challenge: Write a program which finds this number (or a good estimate for it).
See also

import sys
sys.float_info.epsilon

title: Computational Programming with Python
section: What precision do I have at what number
text:
What precision do I have at what number
What decimal precision do I have at a given number \(a \in \mathbb{R}\)?
To figure out the precision we have at a number, we find the interval such that \(a \in [2^k, 2^{k+1})\). We then subdivide that range using the significand bits.
Example: \(3.5 \in [2,4)\). A float in Python has 52 bits of significand, so the precision we have at 3.5 is:
\[(4-2) 2^{-52} = \frac{2}{4503599627370496} \approx 0.00000000000000044408921\]
\(3.5\) itself is actually exactly representable by a float, but the amount of precision numbers we have at that scale is that value. The smallest number you can add or subtract to a value between \(2\) and \(4\) is that value. That is the resolution of the values you are working with when working between \(2\) and \(4\) using a float.

prec = (4-2) * 2**-52
print(f"prec for 3.5 is {prec}")


What decimal precision do I have at \(13689.0\)?
What is the largest possible floating point number in this double precision representation?
What is the smallest gap between floating point numbers around zero?

5min, let’s go!

prec = (2**14 - 2**13)* 2**-52
print(f"prec for 13689 is {prec}")

largest = 2**1023
print(f"Largest floating point number: {largest:2.4e}")

smallest = 2**-1023
print(f"Distance between 0 and next number: {smallest:2.4e}")

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Internal representation (cont.)
The smallest positive representable number is \[
\mathrm{fl_{min}} = 1 \cdot 2^{-1023} \approx 10^{-308}
\] and the largest is \[
\mathrm{fl_{max}} = 1.111 \dots 1 \cdot 2^{1023} \approx 10^{308}.
\]
Floating point numbers are not equally spaced in \([0, \mathrm{fl_{max}}]\).
Gap at zero (caused by normalization \(x_0 \neq 0\)):
Distance between \(0\) and the first positive number is \(2^{-1023}\).
Distance between the first and the second is smaller by a factor \(2^{-52}\).



floatz.png

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Infinite and Not a Number
There are in total \(2(\beta-1)\beta^{t-1}(2k_{max} + 1) + 1\) floating point numbers, in short floating point numbers are limited.
Numbers bigger than the maximal floating point number \(\mathrm{fl_{max}}\) generate in numpy an inf or an overflow exception.
Numbers smaller than the minimal floating point number \(\mathrm{fl_{min}}\) generate subnormalized numbers or not a number, short nan. This leads to unexpected behavior.

x = nan
print(x < 0)
print(x > 0)
print(x == x)

The float inf behaves much more as expected:

print(0 < inf)
print(inf <= inf)
print(inf == inf)
print(-inf < inf)
print(inf - inf)
print(exp(-inf))
print(exp(1/inf))

title: Computational Programming with Python

Creating sublists - Slicing
Slicing a list between index \(i\) and \(j\) is forming a new list by taking elements starting at \(i\) and ending just before \(j\).

Example

L = ['C', 'l', 'o', 'u', 'd']

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Partial slicing
One may omit the first or the last bound of the slicing:

L = ['C', 'l', 'o', 'u', 'd']
print("L[1:] =", L[1:])     # to the end
print("L[:3] =", L[:3])     # from the start
print("L[-2:] =", L[-2:])   # negative index
print("L[:-2] =", L[0:-2])

L[1:] = ['l', 'o', 'u', 'd']
L[:3] = ['C', 'l', 'o']
L[-2:] = ['u', 'd']
L[:-2] = ['C', 'l', 'o']



Mathematical analogy
The interval \([-\infty, a)\) means: take all numbers strictly lower than \(a\), cf. syntax of L[:j].

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
To sum it up

L[i:] take all elements except the \(i\) first ones
L[:i] take the first \(i\) elements
L[-i:] take the last \(i\) elements
L[:-i] take all elements except the \(i\) last ones

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
for loops (revisited)
A for loop allows to loop through a list using an index variable. This variable takes succesively the values of the elements in the list.
Example:

L = [1, 2, 10] 
for s in L:
    print(s * 2)
    print("Hello", s)
    
print("Loop finished")

2
Hello 1
4
Hello 2
20
Hello 10
Loop finished



Repeating a task
One typical use of the for loop is to repeat a certain task a fixed number of times:

def do_something(i):
    print(i)
    
n = 10 
for i in range(n):
    do_something(i) # this gets executed n times



Indentation
The part to be repeated in the for loop has to be properly indented.
for elt in my_list:
    do_something()
    something_else()
    etc
print("loop finished") # outside of the for loop
In contrast to other programming languages, the indentation in Python is mandatory.
Many other kinds of Python structures also have to be indented and this will be covered when introduced.

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
The full for statement ‐ break
break gets out of the for loop before all elements of the list are used.
In the following example we possibly don’t use all values of the list x_values.

x_values=[0,2,3,4,5]
threshold=3.5
for x in x_values:
    if x > threshold:
        break
    print(x)

0
2
3


Not all entries were visited. We say, the list was not exhausted.

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:

else checks if the loop was not broken by the break keyword.

threshold=6
for x in x_values:
    if x > threshold:
        break
    #else:
    #    print("all the x are below the threshold")   
    print(x)  
else:
    print("all the x are below the threshold")

2
3
4
5
all the x are below the threshold


If we did not break, the else-block is executed.

Fixed point iterations
A recursive equation can be written as
\[\begin{cases}
a_0 &= c \\
a_{n+1} &= f(a_n), n \ge 0
\end{cases}\]

a = c              # some initial value c
n = 100            # for some n
for i in range(n): 
    a = f(a)       # where f is some function

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Fixed point
A number \(x_0\) such that \(f(x_0)=x_0\) is called a fixed point.
The sequence will converge to that fixed point if \(f\) is a contraction (\(|f(x) - f(y)| < \alpha |x - y| \ \forall x,y\) and \(\alpha \in [0,1)\)) and a self map onto a closed set (see Banach’s fixed point theorem).
An example is visualised using a cob web diagram, see www.geogebra.org/m/za7tarfg. Here you see that a fixed point can be repelling or attracting. If the initial value \(c\) is "close to" an attracting fixed point (\(f\) is a contraction), the sequence will converge to that fixed point.

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
NumPy arrays ‐ vectors

The array type
Lists are almost like vectors but operations on lists are not linear algebra operations.

L1 = [1, 2]
L2 = [3, 4]
print("L1 + L2 =", L1 + L2)
print("3*L1 =", 3*L1)


Definition
An array represents a vector or a matrix in linear algebra. It is often initialised from a list or another vector. Operations +, *, /, - are all elementwise. dot or the @ operator are used for the scalar product.

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Vector usage

Example

from numpy import array, dot, sqrt, inf
from scipy.linalg import norm

vec = array([3, -4]) # a vector in the plane

print("vec =", vec)
print("2*vec =", 2*vec)
print("vec*vec =", vec*vec)
print("vec/2 =", vec/2) 
print("vec/vec =", vec/vec) 

# TODO: explain norms 
print("||vec|| =", norm(vec, ord=2))
print("|vec| = ", sqrt(dot(vec,vec))) # same as norm(vec, ord=2)

# TODO: explain
print("scalar product =", dot(vec, vec))
print("scalar product =", vec @ vec)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Vectors are similar to lists

L1 = [1, 2, 3]

v1 = array(L1)

print("L1 =", L1)
print("v1 =", v1)
print(type(L1))
print(type(v1))

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Vectors are similar to lists (cont)

Acess vectors via their indices


v = array([1, 2, 3])

print(v[0])


The length of a vector is still obtained by the function len


print(len(v))

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Vectors are similar to lists (cont)

Parts of vectors using slices


v = array([1, 2, 3])
print(v[:2])


Replace parts of vectors using slices


v[:2] = [10, 20]
print(v)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Vectors are not lists!
Operations are not the same:

Operations + and * are different
More operations are defined: -, /
Numpy functions act elementwise on vectors: sin, exp, sqrt, etc.
Scalar product with dot or @
Vectors have a fixed size: no append method!

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Vectors are not lists! (cont)
Two names are bound to the same list:

L1 = [1, 2]
L2 = L1
L1[0] = 10
print(L2)
L2[0] = 4
print(L1)

To make an actual copy, you can use the copy method, or make a slice.

L1 = [1, 2] # compare with with numpy array (next silde)
L2 = L1 
L3 = L1.copy()
L4 = L1[:]  # a slice of the entire list
L1[0] = 10  # what happens here? 
print("L2 =", L2)
print("L3 =", L3)
print("L4 =", L4)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Vectors are not lists! (cont)

Vector slices, on the other hand, are views:


L1 = [1, 2, 3]

v1 = array([1, 2, 3])

L2 = L1[:2]
L2[0] = 10
print("now L1 = ", L1)

v3 = v1[:2]
#v3[0] = 10
print("now v1 = ",v1)

v2 = v1[:2]
v2[0] = 10
print("now v1 = ", v1)

v3 = v1.copy()[:2]
v3[0] = 10
print("now v3 = ", v3)

Only one type throughout the entire vector



v1 = array([1, 2., 3.]) # don't forget the dots!
print(v1)
v2 = array([2, 0, 1])    # one dot is enough

print(v2)

print(v1*v2)  # what about v1/v2

print(3*v1 + 2*v2)

print(v2)

print(type(v1[0]))
print(type(v2[0]))

v1 = array([1., 2., 3.])

print("scalar product:", v1 @ v2)

# access
v1[0] = 10
print("v1 =", v1)

# slices
v1[:2] = [0, 1]

Some handy functions to quickly create vectors:

v1 = zeros(5)
print("v1 =", v1)

v2 = ones(3)
print("v2 =", v2)

v3 = full(4, 3.14)  # fill it with the value 3.14
print("v3 =", v3)

Creating random vectors
Fill a vector with random numbers in the interval [0, 1).

v1 = random.random(5)
print(v1) 

We can also shuffle the values in an array.

v2 = array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 80])

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Concatenating vectors
Since the + operation is redefined, we need other means to concatenate vectors.
The command hstack([v1, v2, ..., vn]) concatenates the vectors \(v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\).

v1 = [1, 2, 3]
v2 = [4, 5]
v3 = [6, 7, 8, 9]

L = v1 + v2 + v3
print(L)
v = hstack([array(v1), v2, v3])
# w = vstack([v1, v2, v3])
print(v)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Functions and arrays
As long as +, -, *, / and standard mathematical numpy functions are used, a function value can be calculated elementwise.

def my_func(x, A, omega):
    return A*sin(omega*x)/x

x = linspace(-100, 100, 200) # using an even number of values to avoid zero
A = [2 for i in range(200)] # full(100, 2)
y = my_func(x, A, 0.5)
plot(x, y)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Vectorized functions
Note that not all functions may be applied to vectors. For instance this one:

def const(x):
    return 1

x = linspace(-100, 100, 50)
y = const(x) 

# what is the value of y?
print(y)

We will see later how to automatically vectorize a function so that it works on vectors.

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
NumPy arrays ‐ matrices

Definition
Matrices are represented by arrays of lists of rows, which are lists as well.

# An identity matrix
id_matrix = array([[1., 0.], [0., 1.]])

# Python allows this:
id_matrix = array([[1., 0],
                   [0., 1.]])

# Which is more readable?

print(id_matrix)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Accessing matrix entries
Matrix elements are accessed with two indices.

M = array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])

print(M[0, 0])  # first row, first column

print(M[-1, 0]) # last row, first column

# Don't do this:
print(M[0][0])
print(M[0])

Compare this to accessing list elements.

L = [[1., 2.], [3., 4.]]

print(L[0][0])

print(L[-1][0])

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Creating matrices ‐ eye, zeros, full

eye(n) is the identity matrix of size \(n\).
zeros([n, m]) fills an \(n\times m\) matrix with zeroes
full([n, m], value)fills an \(n\times m\) matrix with value


id_matrix = eye(100)
M0 = zeros((2, 3))     # using a list [2, 3]
M1 = full((2, 3), 7.)  # using a tuple (2, 3)

print(id_matrix)
print(M0, '\n')
print(M1)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Creating random matrices

M1 = random.random((3, 4))
print(M1)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Shape
The shape of a matrix is the tuple of its dimensions. The shape of an \(n\times m\) matrix is (n,m). It is given by the attribute shape:

M = eye(3) 
print(M.shape)
V = array([1., 2., 1., 4.])
print(V.shape)               # tuple with one element


Tip
zeros(A.shape) returns a matrix with the same shape as A containing only zeros.

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Transpose
The transpose of a matrix \(A\) is a matrix \(B\) such that
\[B_{ij} = A_{ji}.\]
By transposing a matrix you switch the two shape elements.

A = array([[1, 2, 3],
           [4, 5, 6]])
print("A.shape =", A.shape)
print(A[1,2])

B = A.T  # A transpose
print("B.shape =", B.shape, '\n')

#B[0,0] = 11
print("A =")
print(A, '\n')
print("B =")
print(B)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
1D vectors and 2D row/column matrices
(here D stands for tensor dimension, i.e. the length of shape)

from numpy import array 
v = array([1, 2, 3])

Mcol = array([[1], 
              [2], 
              [3]])
Mrow = array([[1, 2, 3]])

print("v.shape = ", v.shape)
print("Mcol.shape = ", Mcol.shape)
print("Mrow.shape = ", Mrow.shape)

print(Mcol)
print(Mrow)
print(Mrow.T)

Transposing a 1D vector doesn’t change it

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Matrix multiplication
We can use the dot function for matrix multiplication. We can also use the @ operator.
If \(A\) is a \(n\times m\) matrix and \(B\) a \(m \times p\) matrix, then \(AB\) is a \(n\times p\) matrix.

from numpy import dot
A = array([[1, 0, 0],        # n = 2, m = 3
           [2, -1, 3]])
B = array([[2, 1, 0, 4],     # m = 3, p = 4
           [1, 1, -1, 0],
           [0, 1, 2, 2]])

  

AB = dot(A, B)
print(AB)

# same as 
AB = A @ B
print(AB)

# BA = dot(B, A)  # error

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Matrix vector multiplication
A matrix can be multipled with a vector using dot or the @ operator. The multiplication is matrix multiplication, as if the vector was a column or row matrix. The result is a vector.
\[
\left(
\begin{array}{rr}
1 & 2
\end{array}
\right)
\left(
\begin{array}{rr}
1 & 0 \\
4 & -1
\end{array}
\right)
=
\left(
\begin{array}{rr}
9 & -2
\end{array}
\right)
\]
\[
\left(
\begin{array}{rr}
1 & 0 \\
4 & -1
\end{array}
\right)
\left(
\begin{array}{rr}
1 \\
2
\end{array}
\right)
=
\left(
\begin{array}{rr}
1 \\
2
\end{array}
\right)
\]

A = array([[1, 0],
           [4, -1]])
v = array([1, 2])

vA = dot(v, A)
vA = v @ A
Av = dot(A, v)

print(vA)
print(Av)
print("vA.shape =", vA.shape, " Av.shape = ", Av.shape)

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Dot product and @ operator









vector vector
\(s = \sum_i x_i y_i\)
s = x @ y or s = dot(x,y)
scalar product




matrix matrix
\(C_{ij} = \sum_k A_{ik}B_{kj}\)
C = A @ B or C = dot(A, B)
matrix multiplication


matrix vector
\(y_i = \sum_j A_{ij}x_j\)
y = A @ x or y = dot(A, x)
matrix multiplication, treating vector as column matrix


vector matrix
\(y_j = \sum_i x_i A_{ij}\)
y = x @ A or y = dot(x, A)
matrix multiplication, treating vector as row matrix

text:
Linear transformations ‐ rotation matrix in the plane

Definition
A linear transformation in the plane is a function \(f:\mathbb{R}^2 \mapsto \mathbb{R}^2\) such that
\(f(a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{v}) = af
(\mathbf{u}) + bf(\mathbf{v}) \text{ for all }a, b\in\mathbb{R} \text{ and } \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2\)

title: Computational Programming with Python
Computational Programming with Python
section: Finding the transformation matrix of a rotation in the plane
text:
Finding the transformation matrix of a rotation in the plane
Let \(\mathbf{e_1}, \mathbf{e_2}\) be two basis vectors and let \(A\) be a transformation matrix that rotates a vector \(\mathbf{u} = x\mathbf{e_1} + y\mathbf{e_2}\) by an angle $$. To find \(A\) it suffices to consider the basis vectors.



rotated basis


Now $ A = xA + yA = x’ + y’$

Rotate a point

from matplotlib.pyplot import *
from numpy import *
%matplotlib inline
alpha = pi/2
A = array([[cos(alpha), -sin(alpha)],
           [sin(alpha), cos(alpha)]])
x = 3
y = 3
P = array([x, y]) # a vector
AP = dot(A, P)    # a vector
AP = A @ P 
plot(x, y, 'bo')
xlim(-5, 5)
ylim(-5, 5)
grid()
plot(*AP, 'ro')  # unpack to get x and y



Rotate many points
5min, let’s go!

alpha = pi/2
A = array([[cos(alpha), -sin(alpha)],
           [sin(alpha), cos(alpha)]])
x = linspace(-10, 10, 200)
y = sin(3*x)
M = array([x, y]) # 2 times 200 matrix
AM = dot(A, M)    # 2 times 200 matrix
plot(x, y)
grid()
plot(*AM)  # unpack to get a x-list and a y-list

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Fixed point iterations
A recursive equation can be written as
\[\begin{cases}
a_0 &= c \\
a_{n+1} &= f(a_n), n \ge 0
\end{cases}\]

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: Computational Programming with Python
text:
Fixed point
A number \(x_0\) such that \(f(x_0)=x_0\) is called a fixed point.
The sequence will converge to that fixed point if \(f\) is a contraction (\(|f(x) - f(y)| < \alpha |x - y| \ \forall x,y\) and \(\alpha \in [0,1)\)) and a self map onto a closed set (see Banach’s fixed point theorem).
An example is visualised using a cob web diagram, see www.geogebra.org/m/za7tarfg. Here you see that a fixed point can be repelling or attracting. If the initial value \(c\) is "close to" an attracting fixed point (\(f\) is a contraction), the sequence will converge to that fixed point.
